title: Phase 11: Cloud deployment and production hardening
description: Project: Phase 11: Cloud deployment and production hardening. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Moving the expense platform to the cloud is not just about provisioning virtual machines. It is about designing for failure, securing data in transit and at rest, and ensuring the application degrades gracefully when a dependency fails. Production hardening is the gap between a demo that works and a system that customers can rely on.

A production-grade cloud deployment uses multiple availability zones, automated scaling, and a content delivery network for static assets. The expense platform API runs behind an application gateway or load balancer, the background worker runs as a separate scalable service, and the database uses a managed service with automated backups and failover.

data.title: Production architecture components
items: Availability zones: deploy across at least two zones to survive a data center failure
Managed database: use Azure SQL or Amazon RDS with automated backups and point-in-time restore
Object storage: store receipt images in blob storage with a CDN for fast global access
Application gateway: terminate TLS, route traffic, and provide WAF protection
Auto-scaling: scale the API and worker based on CPU, memory, or queue depth
Secrets manager: inject database passwords and API keys at runtime
DNS: use a managed DNS service with health checks and automatic failover

terms.definition: An isolated location within a cloud region that has independent power, cooling, and networking to improve fault tolerance.
A distributed network of servers that caches content close to users, reducing latency and origin load.
A security layer that filters and monitors HTTP traffic to protect against common exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
Measures that detect and mitigate distributed denial-of-service attacks, often provided at the cloud provider level.
Managing and provisioning infrastructure through declarative code files rather than manual configuration.
An approach where servers are never modified after deployment; updates are delivered by replacing the entire instance.

data.text: Security in production is defense in depth. Every layer should protect the one below it. The cloud provider secures the physical infrastructure, the network layer restricts traffic, the application validates input, and the database encrypts data at rest. If any one layer fails, the others still protect the system.

items.text: Enable HTTPS everywhere with a valid TLS certificate and HSTS header
items.hint: Use the cloud provider's certificate manager or Let's Encrypt for automated renewal.

items.text: Restrict inbound traffic to ports 443 and 80 at the network security group level
items.hint: Allow SSH or RDP only from known bastion host IPs.

items.text: Encrypt data at rest in the database, blob storage, and backups
items.hint: Use provider-managed keys or customer-managed keys for sensitive data.

items.text: Enable the Web Application Firewall with rules for OWASP Top 10
items.hint: Review WAF logs regularly and tune rules to reduce false positives.

items.text: Rotate database credentials and API keys on a 90-day schedule
items.hint: Automate rotation with the secrets manager; never commit secrets to source control.

items.text: Enable DDoS protection at the cloud provider level
items.hint: Configure rate limiting at the application gateway or load balancer.

items.text: Audit access logs for the database, storage, and management plane
items.hint: Send audit logs to a centralized, immutable log store.

data.text: Manual cloud configuration is a liability. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools such as Terraform, Pulumi, or Azure Bicep let you define the entire environment in version-controlled files. The environment can be recreated from scratch, reviewed in pull requests, and audited for drift.

cards.title: Terraform
cards.description: Declarative infrastructure as code with a large provider ecosystem.

cards.title: Pulumi
cards.description: Infrastructure as code using real programming languages such as C# or TypeScript.

cards.title: Azure Bicep
cards.description: A domain-specific language for deploying Azure resources.

data.text: IaC should be reviewed and tested like application code. Use tflint or Pulumi's policy engine to catch misconfigurations before they reach production. Run security scans on your infrastructure code to detect open security groups, unencrypted storage, or overprivileged identities.

data.title: IaC quality tools
items: TFLint: a Terraform linter that catches errors and enforces best practices
Checkov: a static analysis tool for infrastructure as code
Pulumi ESC: centralized secrets and configuration management
tfsec: security scanning for Terraform code
Git hooks: prevent commits with IaC errors using pre-commit hooks

data.title: Immutable infrastructure over hotfixes
data.text: When a server misbehaves in production, the temptation is to SSH in and fix it. That creates configuration drift and makes the system impossible to reproduce. Fix the image or IaC definition, redeploy, and terminate the old instance.

items.question: How do I handle secrets in infrastructure as code?
items.answer: Never hardcode secrets in IaC files. Reference secrets by name from a secrets manager. The IaC tool should have read-only access to the secrets it needs, and all access should be audited.

items.question: What is the difference between a managed database and self-hosted?
items.answer: Managed databases handle patching, backups, and failover automatically. Self-hosted databases give you more control but require you to operate them. For most applications, a managed database is the right choice because it reduces operational burden and improves reliability.

items.question: How do I test infrastructure changes safely?
items.answer: Use a staging environment that mirrors production. Run automated tests that validate the deployed configuration matches the IaC definition. Use policy-as-code tools such as OPA to enforce security and compliance rules before deployment.

items.question: What is infrastructure drift and how do I prevent it?
items.answer: Drift occurs when the actual cloud state differs from the IaC definition. Run a drift detection job on a schedule and alert on discrepancies. Prevent drift by making all changes through IaC pull requests, never through the cloud console.

data.title: Provision the expense platform in the cloud
data.description: Use Terraform or Pulumi to define the complete production infrastructure for the expense platform, including the App Service, SQL Database, Redis Cache, Storage Account, and Key Vault.
steps: Create a Terraform or Pulumi project for the expense platform
Define the resource group, App Service Plan, and Linux Web App for the API
Add an Azure SQL Server and database with firewall rules and encryption
Add a Redis Cache and Storage Account for receipts
Reference secrets from Key Vault in the App Service configuration
Run terraform plan or pulumi preview and verify the changes
Apply the infrastructure and verify the API is reachable
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a fully provisioned cloud environment defined entirely in code, with no manual configuration steps.

data.title: Summary
points: Deploy across multiple availability zones for fault tolerance
Use a managed database with automated backups and failover
Secure every layer: TLS, WAF, network groups, and encrypted storage
Define all infrastructure as code in version control
Automate security scanning and drift detection
data.takeaway: Production hardening is not a checklist you finish; it is a discipline you maintain. Every new feature should be evaluated for its impact on security, reliability, and operational cost.
